---
title: "Quiz: Dijkstra and live-wire"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Pixels are nodes of a grid graph; a path pays the costs of the pixels (or links) it uses; Dijkstra repeatedly makes the unfinished pixel with the smallest tentative cost final.

---

**Q1.** Why can the row-by-row DP table not find the cheapest path when moves in all four directions are allowed?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The table needs an order in which every value is computed after the values it depends on. With moves in all directions, the best path to a pixel may come from a pixel **below** it (or to its right), which the row order computes later, and that pixel may in turn depend on the first one. No fixed order works in general.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why is the unfinished pixel with the smallest tentative cost already final?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where must any other path to it leave the set of final pixels, and what does that cost?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Any other path to it must leave the final pixels through some unfinished pixel, which already has a tentative cost at least as large; the rest of that path can only **add** cost (all costs are non-negative). So no other path can be cheaper.
:::

---

**Q3.** After Dijkstra has run from a seed, how do you get the cheapest path to a pixel the mouse points at? Why is that fast?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Follow the stored predecessors from the pixel back to the seed (backtracking) and reverse. It takes as many steps as the path is long: no new shortest-path computation, so the live-wire can follow the mouse in real time. The expensive part, the tree, is computed once per seed.
:::

---

**Q4.** Name the three terms of the live-wire local cost and what each one rewards.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Gradient magnitude**: strong edges are cheap. **Laplacian zero crossing**: the centre of the edge (where the second derivative changes sign) is cheap, so the wire sits on the edge, not beside it. **Gradient direction**: running **along** the edge direction is cheap, cutting across it is expensive; this keeps the wire smooth and on one edge.
:::

---

**Q5.** The wire cuts across the inside of a cell instead of following its faint boundary. Why, and what do you do?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The cost is a **sum** along the path: a long path along a weak edge can cost more than a short path across a uniform region. Place an **anchor** on the boundary (shorter pieces), or make the edge terms count more relative to the constant per-pixel cost.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why does Dijkstra need non-negative weights, and why is that no problem for live-wire?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With a negative weight, a later detour could lower the cost of a pixel that was already declared final, so "smallest is final" breaks. The live-wire cost terms (gradient, zero crossing, direction, plus a small constant) are all $\ge 0$ by construction.
:::

---

**Q7.** Dijkstra and watershed flooding use the same priority queue. What is the difference in what they minimise?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Dijkstra minimises the **sum** of the costs along a path. Watershed flooding minimises the **maximum** height along a path (the lowest pass between a pixel and a marker). Both process pixels from the queue in increasing order of their value.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* What is the running time of Dijkstra on an $n \times n$ image with 8 neighbours and a binary heap?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$N = n^2$ pixels and about $8N$ edges; each pop and each update costs $O(\log N)$: $O(N \log N) = O(n^2 \log n)$.
:::
